sections.title: First-Order vs. Second-Order Thinking
sections.content: First-order thinking is simple and immediate: 'X will lead to Y.' Second-order thinking asks 'And then what?' — tracing the chain of consequences beyond the obvious first effect. Great debaters and decision-makers distinguish themselves by thinking in second-order terms.
bullets: First-order: 'We lower taxes, so people have more money.'
Second-order: 'People have more money, which increases demand, which causes inflation, which erodes the value of their money.'
The best arguments anticipate second and third-order effects

sections.title: The 'And Then What?' Framework
sections.content: Second-order thinking is a simple habit: after identifying an outcome, ask 'And then what happens?' Repeat this 2-3 times to uncover hidden consequences that your opponent probably hasn't considered.
bullets: Every policy has intended effects (first-order) and unintended effects (second-order+)
Opponents usually argue only about first-order effects
Second-order arguments show deeper analysis and win judge credibility

sections.title: Second-Order Thinking in Action
sections.content: Motion: 'This house would implement rent control.'
sections.good:
First-order: Rent control keeps housing affordable.
Second-order: Landlords earn less profit, so they build fewer new units, which reduces housing supply, which increases competition for existing units, which drives UP prices for non-controlled units.
Third-order: The overall housing shortage worsens, hurting the very people rent control was designed to help.
sections.explanation: The second and third-order analysis reveals that a well-intentioned policy can backfire. This depth of analysis is far more persuasive than simply debating the first-order effect.

sections.instruction: A city builds a new highway to reduce traffic congestion. What is a likely second-order effect?
options: People move further from the city, increasing total driving distance and eventually refilling the highway
The highway pays for itself in tolls
sections.feedback: The second-order effect is induced demand — easier driving encourages more driving and suburban sprawl, eventually leading to the same congestion levels.

sections.q: What distinguishes second-order thinking from first-order thinking?
options: Second-order thinking traces the chain of consequences beyond the obvious first effect
Second-order thinking only applies to economics
sections.explain: Second-order thinking asks 'And then what?' repeatedly to uncover hidden consequences that simple first-order analysis misses.

sections.statement: First-order effects are always more important than second-order effects when evaluating a policy.
sections.feedback: Second-order effects are often larger and more important than first-order effects. The most significant consequence of a policy is frequently an unintended one.

sections.sentence: The key question for second-order thinking is: '{0} {1} {2}?'
sections.feedback: Keep asking 'And then what?' to trace the chain of consequences deeper.

questions.scenario: A government introduces a subsidy for electric vehicles to reduce emissions.
questions.question: What is a second-order consequence the government should consider?
options: Increased electricity demand may require more power plants, potentially increasing overall emissions if the grid uses fossil fuels
Gas stations will go out of business
questions.feedback: The second-order effect is that EV subsidies shift emissions from tailpipes to power plants. If the grid runs on coal, total emissions might not decrease.

questions.q: Why do skilled debaters use second-order arguments?
options: They reveal hidden consequences that opponents haven't considered, giving a strategic advantage
They are required by debate rules
questions.feedback: Second-order arguments show deeper analysis and catch opponents off guard because they typically only prepare first-order responses.
